groups.title: Moti del basso: diatonic, rising stepwise
groups.blurb: Bass motion only. The bass rises by step; the upper voices are set with a repeating interval pattern.

groups.title: Moti del basso: diatonic, descending stepwise
groups.blurb: The bass falls by step. These are the alternatives to the descending Rule of the Octave.

groups.title: Moti del basso: chromatic, rising
groups.blurb: Chromatic leading tones in the bass make each segment a small cadence in a new key.

groups.title: Moti del basso: chromatic, descending (laments)
groups.blurb: The chromatic tetrachord ①–⑤ in the bass: Lamento and Morte.

groups.title: Moti del basso: disjunct (sequences)
groups.blurb: Sequential basses. A model (prototype) is transposed by a second up or down; the Romanesca is the exception (down a third). Swapping the metric position of bass and chords ("metric inversion") creates a different pattern: A→B ≠ B→A.

groups.title: Schemata: Romanesca, Prinner and opening gambits
groups.blurb: Schemata = a bass motion plus a set of upper voices. Embellishment by suspensions, non-chord tones, bass motion and combinations.

groups.title: Schemata: changing-note (dichotomous) schemata
groups.blurb: Double-neighbour melodic shapes split into a question (opening) and an answer (closing). Aprile, Meyer and paired Do-Re-Mi can sound simultaneously.

groups.title: Schemata: Folia, Fonte, Monte, Monte Romanesca
groups.blurb: Larger sequential schemata, typically opening the second half of a binary form.

groups.title: Schemata on pedal points: Quiescenza, Ponte, Indugio, Fenaroli
groups.blurb: Pedal points on ①, ⑤ or ④ with stereotyped chord successions.

groups.title: Combinations of schemata
groups.blurb: Schemata chained into phrases; harmonic rhythm often accelerates.

groups.title: Rule of the Octave (reference)
groups.blurb: Added from Sanguinetti. Your notes mark several patterns "move to R.O."; this group gives the standard (Fenaroli) Rule of the Octave and the "essential foundations of the key" it is built on, so those links have a target.

groups.title: Suspensions (legature): the four dissonances
groups.notesPages: — (Durante Regole pp. 6–13, 23–24, 38–41; Fenaroli Book III “Delle Dissonanze”)
groups.blurb: Added from the Neapolitan rule books. In partimento theory only suspensions count as dissonances (passing 7ths etc. belong to diminution). For each dissonance the masters list: the consonance that prepares it, the bass motion that produces it, the consonance that accompanies it, and where it resolves with a stationary or a moving bass. Learn these and you can find the suspensions in an unfigured bass.

groups.title: Diminution (Durante, Partimenti diminuiti)
groups.notesPages: — (Durante Partimenti diminuiti; Sanguinetti Ch. 12; Fenaroli Books I, II, IV, V editor notes)
groups.blurb: Added from Durante’s Partimenti diminuiti: each partimento is preceded by two to five “modi” (styles) of embellishing one passage, which the player then applies to every parallel passage. Diminution turns the chordal realization into a fast, idiomatic right-hand line without changing the underlying harmony and voice leading.

patterns.name: 5–6 (stepwise Monte)
patterns.summary: Each bass note carries a 5/3 then a 6/3. The sixth is tied over and becomes the fifth of the next bar, so the potential parallel fifths are broken up.
rules: The 6 on each bass note is held into the next bar as its 5 (tie).
In 3 parts, one upper voice moves in parallel thirds (tenths) with the bass; the other does the 5–6.
guidelines: Major: can span the whole octave.
Minor: usually breaks off after ④ and closes ⑤ (5–7) → ①.
Invertible: 6↔3 and 4↔5 (green marks in notes p.1).

examples.title: Minor, 3 parts, closing ⑤ 5–7 → ①
examples.caption: Melodic-minor inflections (F♯, G♯) follow the rising bass, as in the notes.

sources.fenaroli: Book III, “Moves of the partimento”: rising stepwise I (5th moving to 6th)
sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Ascending 5–6 (Ex. 9.32)
sources.napoli: Durante, Regole p. 26 "Quando ascende vuole 5a e poi 6a"; Fenaroli, Regole (Partimenti Book III) — Movimenti I “Quinta che passa a sesta”; Durante, Partimenti diminuiti No. 9, 12, 28, 50

checks: HCP: “The Monte is a stepwise ascending sequence, in which 5/3 and 6/3 chords alternate.”
Demeyere: sixth tied to the next fifth; major spans an octave, minor stops after ④ while the bass still rises to ⑤.
Fenaroli III: rising stepwise, rule I = 5th moving to 6th, 6th held as next 5th.

Sanguinetti: the oldest alternative to the RO ("altra maniera"); 5 → 6 on every bass note, third voice in 3rds/10ths with the bass; major covers the octave, minor must stop on ⑤ (augmented 2nd); two beats per bass note; its usual descending partner is 7–6.
(Neapolitan sources) Durante: “when the partimento ascends by step it takes the 5th and then the 6th”; Fenaroli adds that every note keeps its 3rd. Matches the data.

patterns.name: 3–6 progression (3–6 Monte)
patterns.summary: Two-part origin of the Monte: the upper voice alternates a third and a sixth over each bass note, leaping a fourth up and a third down.
rules: Upper voice: 3 → 6 over the same bass note (4th up), then 3 over the next bass note (3rd down).
guidelines: The second type of 3–6 progression is the schema Third Down Second Up (see disjunct moti).
Minor: raise ⑥ and ⑦ when the bass ascends (melodic minor).

variants.name: 3-part 3–6 Monte
variants.description: Three-part setting adding a voice to the 3–6 alternation (5/3 → 6/3 per bass note).
variants.review: The voice assignment of the 3-part version on notes p.1 is ambiguous; no realization generated.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.1; HCP Notes p.1 (§1.2)

checks: HCP Terms: “two types of 3–6 progressions … alternation of thirds and sixths on a stepwise bass … second type is Third Down Second Up.”
flags: 3-part voicing not realized (ambiguous in the notes).

patterns.summary: The octave of each bass note is held as a 7th over the next one, resolves to 6, then leaps up a third to the new octave.
rules: 7 must be prepared (tied) and resolve down by step to 6.
Each resolution is followed by a rising third (back to the octave).
guidelines: Major can span the octave; minor only a fourth.
Minor alternative from ④: 7–6 5 | 9–8 7 | 3/8 (notes p.1).

sources.fenaroli: Book III, rising stepwise II (7th resolving to 6th)
sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Ascending 8⌒7–6 (Ex. 9.33)
sources.napoli: Fenaroli, Regole (Partimenti Book III) — Movimenti II “Settima che risolve a sesta”

checks: Demeyere: “each resolution must be followed by a rising third”; major spans an octave, minor a fourth.
Fenaroli III rule II: octave held as 7th, resolves to 6th, rises a 3rd to the octave.
Sanguinetti: needs three beats per bass note in triple meter, four in duple (the dissonance must be longer); third voice in 3rds/10ths with the bass.
(Neapolitan sources) Fenaroli: on a rising bass the 8 of each note is held as a 7 over the next and resolves to 6, then the voice leaps up a 3rd to the next octave. Matches the (8–)7–6 data.
flags: Range in minor: the notes say the minor version spans only a fourth; Sanguinetti says it "must stop on ⑤" (①–⑤). Check which you mean.

patterns.summary: The tenth of each bass note is held as a 9th over the next, resolves to 8, then leaps to the new tenth. An optional 5–6 in the other voice (□ in the notes) smooths the chord change.
rules: 9 prepared by 10, resolves to 8.
Stop at ⑤: continuing to ⑥–⑦ would double the leading tone (crossed out in notes p.1).
guidelines: Cadence: ⑤ 9–8 7 → ① 3/8.
Minor: add a passing ⑦ (G in A minor) in the middle voice to avoid the augmented second.

examples.title: Major, 3 parts
examples.caption: The second half of each bar shows the optional 5–6 shift in the middle voice.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Ascending 10⌒9–8 (Ex. 9.34)

checks: Demeyere: “The 9–8 pattern breaks off at ⑤, probably to avoid doubling the leading note there”; minor needs an added g¹ to avoid the augmented second.
Sanguinetti: cannot go beyond ⑤ in either mode — matches "stops at ⑤".

patterns.name: (10–)9–8 with leapfrog (Corellian)
patterns.summary: The two upper voices take turns: one resolves 9–8 and then leaps a fourth up to the third of the next bass note, while the other is suspended.
rules: Each octave resolution leaps a 4th up to the 3rd over the next bass note.
Avoid the melodic tritone in the middle voice.
guidelines: The voices cross every bar (that is the “leapfrog”).
Also used under the Folia (notes p.26) and the minor Stabat-Mater-type basses.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Ascending 10⌒9–8 (Ex. 9.34b)

checks: Demeyere: “Each octave resolution leaps a fourth to the third on the next bass note, and the middle voice avoids the melodic tritone.”
Sanguinetti: when the two upper voices are a second apart they overlap and take the suspensions in turn; Fenaroli notates what is heard rather than strict voice leading — the leapfrog version.

patterns.name: (10/8–)9/7–8/6 combined
patterns.summary: The 9–8 and 7–6 chains run simultaneously in the two upper voices, giving a richer harmony.
rules: Both suspensions prepared together (10 and 8) and resolved together (8 and 6).

checks: Demeyere: “(10/8–)9/7–8/6: Both suspension chains run simultaneously.”

patterns.name: Stepwise Romanesca (moto)
aka: alternative for the descending Rule of the Octave
patterns.bass: ①–⑦–⑥–⑤–④–③ (+ ②–① to complete the octave)
patterns.summary: Bass notes alternate 5/3 (strong) and 6/3 (weak). Soprano either in parallel thirds with the bass, or leaping (3rd up, 5th down).
rules: One sonority per bass note: 5/3 on strong, 6/3 on weak beats.
To span the octave append ②–① with 6/3 → 5/3.
Minor: use the natural ⑥ and ⑦ (natural minor).
guidelines: Voices available: 5–6, 3–3 (parallel thirds), 3–6 (leaping).
Inverts with the leaping Romanesca (see Schemata).

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Descending 5–6 (Ex. 9.35)

checks: HCP Terms: stepwise Romanesca usually ①→③; 5/3 on strong, 6/3 on weak beats.
Demeyere: alternative for the descending RO; append ②–① to span an octave; melody stepwise (parallel thirds) or leaping.
Sanguinetti: the descending 5–6 is "a variant of the romanesca"; 5 on the first, 6 on the second note of each pair (fa–mi law); it cannot go beyond ③ — only three pairs.

patterns.name: 7–6 Fauxbourdon
patterns.summary: One upper voice in parallel thirds (tenths) with the bass; the other forms a chain of 7–6 suspensions. Each 6 is the preparation of the next 7.
rules: Each 7 tied from the previous 6 and resolved to 6.
Ends with the compound cadence 7–6(♯) → 8 over ②–①.
guidelines: Embellished fauxbourdon; mirrors the 5–6 Monte in descent (HCP).
Can span a full octave in both modes.
(Sanguinetti, after Cotumacci) The penultimate 6th is major when the bass falls a whole step to the goal; if it falls a half step the 6th is minor.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.2; HCP Notes p.4
sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Descending 7–6 (Ex. 9.37)
sources.napoli: Durante, Regole p. 25 "Quando il partimento discende di grado vuole 7a e poi 6a"; Durante, Regole p. 46–49 "Sequences of 7–6"; Durante, Partimenti diminuiti No. 98, 101, 103

checks: HCP Terms: “The 7–6 Fauxbourdon mirrors the Monte in a descending motion, with 7/3 and 6/3 chords alternating.”
Sanguinetti: standard descending partner of the ascending 5–6; runs through the whole octave; suspensions in the top or inner voice.
(Neapolitan sources) Durante: a stepwise descent takes the 7th and then the 6th. In Diminuiti Nos. 101 and 103 such chains end with a 4/2 on ④ that signals the cadence.

patterns.name: Fauxbourdon (parallel 6/3)
patterns.summary: Chains of 6/3 chords between 5/3 anchors. In your notes this is marked “move to R.O.” (it is the default realization of the stepwise RO without anchors).
rules: Not invertible: exchanging the two upper voices turns their parallel fourths into parallel fifths.
Parallel 5/3 chords must be avoided (parallel fifths/octaves).
guidelines: Begin and end with (5)/3 on ①.
Minor: raised ⑥ and ⑦ ascending, natural descending.
(Sanguinetti) A shorter 6–6 descent that ends on a major 6th causes a scale mutation (the major 6th makes the arrival a new tonic).

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.1 (crossed: “move to R.O.”); HCP Notes p.3
sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Descending 6–6 (Ex. 9.36)

checks: HCP Terms: “Fauxbourdon is … the parallel progression of 6/3 chords”; parallel 5/3 chords must be avoided.
Sanguinetti: first note 5/3 (counts as ①), then 6/3 chords; the last 6th acts as a leading tone and must be major, resolving up to the octave.

patterns.name: 5–6/4+/2–6 (elaborated stepwise Romanesca)
patterns.summary: Each odd bass note takes 5/3 then 6/4+/2; each even bass note takes 6/3. Every pair is a local ④–③ (in V, iii/III and I).
rules: The 4+ resolves up to the 6 of the next bass note; the bass resolves down by step.
guidelines: Usually major.
Your notes ask: “inverted fonte-romanesca?” — Demeyere confirms Byros’s label.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Descending 5–6 with 4/2 (Ex. 9.35c–d)

checks: Demeyere: “Each uneven bass note takes a triad, then a 6/4+/2 chord; each even bass note takes one sixth chord … local ④–③ … typically major … Byros labels it an inverted Fonte-Romanesca.”
Sanguinetti: Fenaroli inserts a 4/2 (augmented 4th) between the triad and the 6th, approached from below or above; only one position (3rd on top).

patterns.name: Chromatic 5–6 (descending)
patterns.summary: Most bass notes take 5/3 then 6/3 with chromatic inflections, tonicizing VI, (V), IV, (III), II on the way down. The upper voices combine a descending chromatic line and an ascending diatonic one.
rules: Each 6 resolves (→8) as a local leading-tone motion into the next key.
guidelines: Contains the Fonte-Romanesca in its first segment.
Several distributions exist (notes p.3 shows two major and three minor versions).

checks: Demeyere: derived from settings by Muscogiuri and Lavigna (not Fenaroli’s regole); Fonte-Romanesca appears in the first excerpt.
flags: Dense chromatic voice distribution: no automatic realization generated; transcribe directly from notes p.3 when building.

patterns.name: Tied bass: (5–)6/4+/2–6(/5)
patterns.bass: ① ⑧ ⌒ ⑦ ⌒ ⑥ ⌒ ⑤ ⌒ ④ ⌒ ③ (syncopated)
patterns.summary: The bass is syncopated: each tied bass note is a 2nd (4/2) against the upper voices on the strong beat and resolves down to a 6/3 on the weak beat.
rules: Each tied bass note is a suspension: prepared, sounded against 4/2 (or 6/4/2) on the strong beat, resolved down by step.
At the syncopated ④ the 4 must be augmented (6/4+/2) — “④ MUST w/ 4+”.
The pattern stops on ③; then a cadence (e.g., ② 6/5 – ⑤ – ①).
guidelines: Variant I: 6/4+/2 on every strong beat (scale mutations; local ④→③ in V, IV, iii, I…).
Variant II: diatonic 6/4/2 strong, 6/3 weak.
Variant III: 6/4/2 strong, 6/5/3 weak.
3 parts: drop the 6–8 line → 4/2 – 6/3 (HCP §2.5).
2 parts: 2–6 over the tied bass (HCP §1.4).
Opening gambit: ① ⑧⌒ ⑦♯ → ① with 2–3 / 4–6 figures (notes p.4).

examples.title: Variant II, 4 parts, major
examples.caption: At ④ the 4 is the augmented fourth (diatonic in major). Ends with the compound cadence ② 6/5 → ⑤ 7 → ①.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.4; HCP Notes p.5
sources.fenaroli: Book III “Partimento that descends in ties”
sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Descending 6–6 variants (Ex. 9.36b–c, Tritto)
sources.napoli: Durante, Regole p. 23–24, 30, 40–41, 50–51 "tied basses with 4/2 and #4/2; sequences of 4/2–6"; Fenaroli, Movimenti (Sebastiani MS 22.1.23) no. 11 (falls with ties)

checks: Demeyere: three settings (6/4+/2 + 6; diatonic 6/4/2 + 6; 6/4/2 + 6/5); syncopated ④ requires 6/4+/2; 3-part omits the sixth → 4(+)/2.
HCP Terms: 4/2 on the tied (strong) beat, 6/3 on the weak beat; 3-part variant of the two-part 2–3 schema.
Fenaroli III: descending in ties — the last tied 4th “should definitely be augmented”; don’t descend this way beyond ④.
Sanguinetti: with the tenor in parallel 6ths and the upper voices in 3rds, 5/6 and 4/2 alternate on each bass note — Tritto's "descending scale with diverse figures".
(Neapolitan sources) Durante and Fenaroli: a tied bass takes 2 and 4; perfect 4th if the bass returns, augmented if it goes on down. See the new pattern “Bass suspensions”.

patterns.name: Chromatic Monte (③→⑥)
patterns.summary: Each segment is a local ⑦–① cadence: 6/3 (or 6/5) on the chromatic leading tone, 5/3 on the new local tonic. Tonicizes IV, V, vi.
rules: The chromatic leading tones sit in the bass and rise to the local tonic.
Avoid doubling the leading tone in 4 parts (the struck 8 in notes p.5).
guidelines: Embellish with 4–3 suspensions, or invertible 4–3/9–8 pairs.
Two-segment version ends on ⑤ and also occurs in minor.
Major ③→⑥ equals ⑤→① in the relative minor.
(Sanguinetti) In minor the chromatic ascent fits ⑤–⑧ (Fenaroli, Partimenti Book III: 6 and 6 with false 5th); a full-octave chromatic ascent needs a repeated ③ or a diatonic finish after ⑥.

variants.name: Minor ⑤→①
variants.description: Bass ⑤–⑥–♯⑥–⑦–♯⑦–①; tonicizes VI, VII, i. Can be embellished by 9–8/7–6 or 4–3/9–8 suspensions.
variants.review: Not auto-realized; transcribe from notes p.5.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Ascending Chromatic Motions (Ex. 9.38–9.41)
sources.napoli: Fenaroli, Movimenti (Sebastiani MS 22.1.23) no. 10 (rises by semitone); Furno, Movimenti del Partimento §1–2 (three-voice dispositions); Durante, Partimenti diminuiti No. 27, 55

checks: HCP Terms: chromaticism best in the bass; leading tones support secondary dominants (6/3 or 6/5); usual tonicizations ii, IV, V, vi.
Demeyere: ③, ♯④, ♯⑤ act as local leading notes; Fenaroli links it to major and ends on ⑥.
Sanguinetti: of two notes a half step apart the chromatic (lower, "mi") one takes the 6th, the diatonic one the 5th; in major the chromatic ascent fits ③–⑥ — exactly this schema.
(Neapolitan sources) Fenaroli no. 10 and Furno §1–2 (major ③→⑥, minor ⑤→①); Durante No. 27 treats each pair as leading tone + tonic.

patterns.name: Lamento: (6–)7–6
patterns.summary: Chromatic descent ①→⑤ realized with 7–6 suspensions over each pair of bass notes; ends with ⑥–⑤ as an augmented sixth or a Phrygian half cadence.
rules: Best in 3 parts.
In 4 parts the fourth voice (mostly the tenor) is forced to leap to avoid parallel octaves.
guidelines: ⑥–⑤: augmented sixth (♯④ over ♭⑥, per the RO) or major sixth (Phrygian cadence).
Represents lament / suffering; common as a Baroque basso ostinato.

(Sanguinetti) Two less common alternatives: an early "omnibus" with a voice rising chromatically against the bass from a 10th on ♯⑦ to an augmented 6th on ♭⑥; or 6/3 chords only, ending with an augmented 6th.

examples.title: 3 parts, A minor, ending with the augmented sixth

variants.name: Lamento 6–6 (simplified)
variants.description: Only sixth chords; normally three voices in one position (exchanging the upper voices creates fifths).

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Descending Chromatic Motions (Ex. 9.42a)
sources.napoli: Fenaroli, Movimenti (Sebastiani MS 22.1.23) no. 9 (falls by semitone); Furno, Movimenti del Partimento §3 (three-voice dispositions); Durante, Partimenti diminuiti No. 75

checks: HCP Terms: Lamento fits best in 3 parts; in 4 parts the fourth voice (mostly tenor) must leap to prevent parallel octaves.
Demeyere: chain of 7–6; ⑥–⑤ with augmented sixth or Phrygian cadence; 6–6 version in one position only.
Sanguinetti: the favoured accompaniment of the chromatic ⑧–⑤ descent (passus duriusculus): the 7th falls on the chromatic note and resolves on the diatonic one; slower tempo than the diatonic 7–6.
(Neapolitan sources) Fenaroli no. 9, Furno §3 (falls by semitones ①→⑤). Durante No. 75: 4ths (often augmented) expanding to 6ths over a chromatic descent.

patterns.name: Morte
patterns.summary: Same chromatic bass as the Lamento, different harmony: the upper voice moves in contrary motion; ⑦♭ carries an active 6/4+/2 (④→③ in the IV key); ♭⑥ an augmented sixth.
rules: The 6/4+/2 on the lowered ⑦ resolves to 6/3 on ⑥ (tonicizes IV).
guidelines: Can open a piece (contrary motion between ① and ⑤).
Alternative segment 3 uses a passing 6/4 to avoid parallel fifths.

checks: HCP Terms: Morte shares the Lamento bass; both modes; upper voice in contrary motion; lowered ⑦ supports a secondary 4/2 → 6/3 on ⑥ (IV).
Demeyere: 6/+4/2 on ♭⑦; common in major.

patterns.name: Second up, third down
patterns.summary: Strong beats: 6 or 6/5; weak beats: 5/3.
rules: Bad for opening a piece: it starts on a 6/3 or 6/5 chord.
guidelines: 5/3 on the weak beat sounds unstable → prefer the metric complement, third down second up.
Rare in partimenti because its meter is unclear.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Rising by Step and Falling by Thirds (Ex. 9.45)
sources.napoli: Furno, Movimenti del Partimento §4 (three-voice dispositions)

checks: Demeyere: strong beats 6 or 6/5, weak beats triad; not suitable for opening; rare, tends to sound like Third Down Second Up.
Sanguinetti: sequential form of the rising half step (mi–fa); metrically ambiguous — often heard as "third down, step up".
(Neapolitan sources) Furno §4 (“rises by a step and falls by a third”).

patterns.name: Third down, second up
patterns.summary: Strong beats: 5/3; weak beats: 6 or 6/5. Derived from the two-part 3–6 progression.
rules: Fits the meter (5/3 on the strong beat).
guidelines: Embellish with 10–9–3 suspensions (4 parts) or with (5–)7–6 and (3–)9–8 together (“2 perspectives”).

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Falling by Thirds and Rising by Step (Ex. 9.47)
sources.napoli: Fenaroli, Movimenti (Sebastiani MS 22.1.23) no. 2; Furno, Movimenti del Partimento §6 (three-voice dispositions); Durante, Partimenti diminuiti No. 50, 59, 72, 77–78, 91, 100, 102–103

checks: HCP Terms: Third Down Second Up alternates 6/5 and 5/3 (6/3 may replace 6/5).
Demeyere: usually ①→⑤ or ④→①; triad on strong beats.
Sanguinetti: first note takes the 5th, second the 6th (again mi–fa) — matches "5/3 strong, 6 weak".
(Neapolitan sources) Fenaroli no. 2, Furno §6; Durante usually puts a 6/3 or 6/5/3 on the second note.

patterns.name: Third up, second down
patterns.bass: ①–③ | ②–④ | ③–⑤ | ④–⑥ | ⑤ → ①
patterns.summary: The first bass note of each segment takes a 7–6 suspension, the second a sixth chord.
rules: The first-bass-note suspensions are the defining feature (7–6, or 3–4–3 in the 4-part version).
guidelines: Better in triple time.
4 parts: each falling second becomes a local ②→① clausula tenorizans with a 3–4–3 suspension.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Rising by Thirds and Falling by Step (Ex. 9.46)
sources.napoli: Fenaroli, Movimenti (Sebastiani MS 22.1.23) no. 1; Furno, Movimenti del Partimento §5 (three-voice dispositions); Durante, Partimenti diminuiti No. 11, 15–17, 20, 29, 44, 98

checks: Demeyere version 1: 7–6 on each first bass note, sixth chord on the second; version 2: local ②–① clausula tenorizans with 4–3.
Sanguinetti: two readings — rising by 3rds (the falling note shares the previous harmony) or falling by step (the first note offers a dissonant suspension, the data's 7–6 version).
(Neapolitan sources) Listed as a standard movimento by Fenaroli (no. 1) and Furno (§5).
flags: Sanguinetti's main Fenaroli version (Ex. 9.46a) is NOT accompanied sequentially: the accented notes follow the Rule of the Octave (Fenaroli: "a scale interrupted by the third"). The notes/data present the 7–6 sequential version as the default; consider adding the RO version.

patterns.name: Fourth down, second up (leaping Romanesca / Pachelbel bass)
patterns.summary: Upper voices in parallel thirds; complete and incomplete 5/3 alternate. The only sequence whose model is transposed down a third.
rules: Minor: natural ⑥ and ⑦.
guidelines: (8–)4–3 / (3–)9–8 suspensions are invertible — keep them for 3 parts.
Full schema material (embellishments, stretto, endings) is under Schemata → Leaping Romanesca.

sources.sanguinetti: Sanguinetti, The Art of Partimento (2012), Ch. 9 — Falling by Fourths and Rising by Step = Romanesca (Ex. 9.50)

patterns.name: Leaping Romanesca
patterns.summary: Opening schema; Pachelbel’s Canon is “the” exemplar. Upper voices in parallel thirds; complete and incomplete 5/3 alternate.
rules: Minor uses the natural scale (⑥♮, ⑦♮).
Only complete 5/3 chords → 4 parts required.
guidelines: Suspensions: (5–)4–3 in 2 parts; (8–)4–3 / (3–)9–8 in 3 parts (invertible); add (5–)4–3 for a third chain.

Embellish the embellishments: repeated notes; escape tone (step then leap); repeated notes + escape tone; upper neighbour; double neighbour; lower neighbour + escape tone; arpeggiation (compound line: two voices merged into one); lower neighbour + arpeggio; passing tones; passing tones + arpeggio; rests (offbeat entries); combinations of the above.
If the bass is embellished (chordal skips, Insanguine, Durante or Fenaroli running basses), keep the upper voices plain.
3-part embellishment: one upper voice; or two voices in parallel/complementary (canonic) motion; bariolage as a keyboard technique.
With 6/4+ (Fenaroli): the bass may fall a perfect 4th with 6/4+; with 6/4+/2 the bass must step down.

variants.name: Temporary key change

variants.name: Stretto
variants.description: 2 parts: second voice enters a bar late at the 3rd (stretto sine pausa = without the rest). Stretto per arsin et thesin uses syncopations (9–3). 3 parts: avoid parallel fifths by doubling the 3rd at the end.

variants.name: Modified and shortened end

patterns.name: Stepwise Romanesca
patterns.summary: Stepwise diatonic descent; it is the leaping Romanesca in invertible counterpoint. Often extended by a Prinner (④–③–②–①).
rules: Avoid the incomplete 6/3 with doubled 6th (3↑6 over 8↓6).
Minor: use ⑥♮ and ⑦♮ (natural minor) — less common.
guidelines: 3-part options: 3/8 | 3/6; or 3/5 (invertible); or 3↑6 with 3↓2 voices.
(3–)2–3 suspensions in either voice, or as a syncopated/tied bass.
Temporary key change: ⑦ → ⑥ as 4+ (vi key), ⑤ → ④ (IV key).
Embellishments: same choices as the leaping Romanesca.

checks: HCP: stepwise ↔ leaping Romanesca by invertible counterpoint; suspensions less frequent but possible; natural minor.

patterns.name: Prinner
patterns.summary: The galant riposte: answers an opening gambit. In 3 parts a third voice is nearly stationary on ① (upper voice in the 17th c., middle in the 18th c.).
rules: 5/3 on ④ (deviates from the descending RO).
Modulating Prinner (①–⑦–⑥–⑤ = ④–③–②–① of V) needs ⑥ raised; it does not exist in minor.
guidelines: Best in major (graceful).
With 7–6 on ②: stage 3 twice as long as stage 1.
High ② drop: conventional ornamental sign of impending closure.
Incomplete Prinner: repeat stages 1–2 (④–③, ④–③, ④–③–②–①).

variants.name: Bass ④–③–②–⑤–①

variants.name: Bass ④–③–②–⑦–①

patterns.name: Folia
patterns.summary: Late Folia (17th–18th c.), usually in D minor, in 3/4 with the sarabande rhythm. Bass moves by fourths and seconds; temporary turn to the relative major (♭⑦–♭③).

patterns.name: Suspensions: principles (preparation, accompaniment, resolution)
patterns.summary: Four dissonances: the 2nd, 4th, 7th and 9th. They exist to make the consonances that follow more beautiful, so each must be prepared by a consonance and resolve to one. The 4th, 7th and 9th sit in the upper voices; the 2nd is the bass suspension (the bass note is tied while the upper voices move to it). Dissonance on the strong beat, resolution on the following weak beat.
rules: Every upper-voice dissonance (4, 7, 9) is prepared in the same voice by a consonance on the previous note and resolves down by step.
Preparing consonances: the 4th from 8, 3, 5 or 6 (also from the minor 7th or diminished 5th); the 7th from 8, 3, 5 or 6; the 9th from 3 or 5 only (from 8 it would make parallel octaves).
Accompanying consonances: the 4th always with the 5th (so it can only stand on a bass note that naturally takes a 5th); the 7th with the 3rd; the 9th with the 10th (3rd).
Primary resolution, bass stationary: 4→3, 7→6, 9→8; bass 2→3 (the bass resolves down).
The 2nd and the 9th are different intervals in partimento theory: the 9th must be prepared, the 2nd (bass suspension) needs no preparation in the right hand — it is struck “di botto”.
guidelines: Secondary resolutions (bass moves while the dissonance resolves): 7→3 when the bass rises a 4th / falls a 5th; 9→3 when the bass falls a 3rd / rises a 6th; 9→6 when the bass rises a 3rd / falls a 6th; 4→6 when the bass falls a 4th.

Suspensions are harmonically placed: the 4–3 prepared by the 8 is the compound cadence; the 7–6 is the tenor clausula ②→①; the 9–8 usually stands on ④ (sometimes on ①). In sequences they are free of these tonal constraints.
(Sanguinetti, Table 9.4) Secondary accompaniments: 4th with 6th; 9th with 5th. Add the 5th to a 9th only when it is isolated, or when the 5th moves to 6 before the next 9th — otherwise parallel 5ths.

Practice order (Fenaroli Book II, editor’s notes): first make every suspension correctly prepared and resolved; then find places for motives; finally shape whole phrases and connect sequences with rising or falling lines.
Fenaroli: the minor 7th and diminished 5th count as consonances (they need no preparation); Pasquini, earlier, treated the false 5th as a dissonance. Follow the source you are realizing.

patterns.name: The 4th (4–3): six preparations
patterns.bass: bass motion → preparation: up 5th/down 4th → 8 · down step → 3 · up step → 5 · up 3rd → 6 · up 4th → m7 · up semitone → d5
patterns.summary: The most important dissonance: the core of the compound and double cadences. Which consonance prepares the 4th depends only on how the bass moves to the note that carries it, so a bass line tells you where a 4–3 is possible.
rules: From the 8: the bass rises a 5th or falls a 4th (① → ⑤): the compound cadence.
From the 3: the bass falls a step (⑥ → ⑤, or ② → ①).
From the 5: the bass rises a step (④ → ⑤, or ① → ②).
From the 6: the bass rises a 3rd (③ → ⑤).
From the minor 7th: the bass rises a 4th (⑤ → ①). From the diminished 5th: the bass rises a semitone (⑦ → ①).
The 4th is always accompanied by the 5th, and resolves to the 3rd over the same bass note.
guidelines: (Sanguinetti) Secondary resolutions: 4 → diminished 5th when the bass falls a minor 3rd (it then rises a semitone as a new leading tone); 4 → 6 when the bass falls a 4th.
In three parts the suspension can sit in either upper voice; when the 5th would have to cross above the suspended voice, put the 4th in the lower voice (examples c, d).

patterns.bass: up step → 8 · up 4th/down 5th → 3 · up 6th/down 3rd → 5 · down step → 6
patterns.summary: Outside sequences, the suspended 7th belongs to the tenor clausula: it stands on ② (or on ⑤), resolves to a major 6th, and the bass then steps down to ①. From the 3: the bass rises a 4th or falls a 5th (⑥ → ②, ① → ④).
From the 5: the bass rises a 6th or falls a 3rd (④ → ②).
From the 6: the bass falls a step (③ → ②).
The 7th is accompanied by the 3rd. It resolves to the 6th if the bass holds, to the 3rd if the bass rises a 4th / falls a 5th.

patterns.name: Bass suspensions: 4/2 (returning) and 4+/2 (moving on)
patterns.bass: ① ⌒ ⑦ ① (returns) · ① ⌒ ⑦ ⑥ ⑤ (continues down)
patterns.summary: The one suspension the realizer cannot skip, because the bass itself is tied or syncopated: whenever the partimento ties a note, the right hand plays a 2nd and a 4th above it (a 6th may be added), and the bass resolves down by step. Whether the bass then comes back or keeps going decides the quality of the 4th.
rules: A tied or syncopated bass always takes 2 and 4 (± 6); the bass resolves down by step. No figures are needed to know this.
Bass returns to the tied note (neighbour figure): the 4th is perfect (“quarta minore”). Over the resolution the 2nd stays as a 3rd, and the 4th either stays as a diminished 5th or rises to a 6th.
Bass does not return (keeps descending): the 4th is augmented (“quarta maggiore”) and must rise a semitone to the 6th; the 2nd stays as the 3rd.
The augmented-4th suspension moves the harmony to the key of the 5th: the next stepwise-falling bass note is no longer ⑦ of the old key but ③ of the new one.
guidelines: The 6th after the augmented 4th is often tied again over the next bass note as a 7–6, making a tenor clausula into the new key (example c).
In a chain of bass suspensions the 4ths follow the scale; the last one, on ④ going to ③, is augmented. In minor it is raised artificially; Valente allows all of them augmented “per modo cantabile”.
Durante (pp. 30–31): with a chain of ties the bass takes 4/2 each time; if the bass leaps up after a tie, read 5–6 instead of 2–4.

patterns.summary: Durante’s scale (“modulazione dei toni”), a generation before Fenaroli. Compared with Fenaroli’s standard version it is plainer going up — ② and ③ take simple 6ths and ④ a triad — and it repeats ⑤ so the ascent pauses on the dominant. Going down it agrees with Fenaroli on ⑥ (raised 6th leading to ⑤) and ④ (6/4/2). In minor the descending ⑥ takes the augmented 6th.

Descending ⑥ takes the raised (major) 6th that leads to ⑤; descending ④ takes 6/4 = 6/4/2.
Minor, ascending: melodic minor, ♯⑥ with 6, ♯⑦ with 6/5. Descending: natural ⑦ and ⑥, ⑥ with ♯6 (an augmented 6th above the bass), ⑤ major, ④ 6/♯4(/2), ② ♯6.
guidelines: Use Durante’s scale when realizing Durante’s own partimenti; Fenaroli’s fuller figures (② 6/4/3, ④ 6/5/3) are the later Neapolitan standard.

patterns.name: Durante’s interval rules for the bass (mi takes the 6th, etc.)
patterns.figures: rising semitone: lower note 6 · falling semitone: 2nd note 6 (at a close: 5) · M3 → 8 or 6 · M6 → 8 · d5 → 3
patterns.summary: Short rules in Durante’s Regole that let you harmonize an unfigured bass from its intervals alone. They are the reasoning behind the Rule of the Octave: a semitone in the bass marks a “mi” (the lower note of a rising semitone), which takes a 6th.
rules: When the bass rises a semitone, the first note takes the 6th (it is a “mi”: ③ → ④, ⑦ → ①).

When the bass falls a semitone, the second note takes the 6th (④ → ③ with 6 on ③) — but when the falling semitone closes a descent (⑥ → ⑤ in minor, a Phrygian ending), the last note takes the 5th (with a major 3rd).
A major 3rd above the bass rises: to the 8 of the next bass (falling 5ths) or to its 6th.
A major 6th expands to the octave (bass down a step, upper voice up a step).
A diminished 5th contracts to a 3rd (bass up a semitone, upper voice down a step).
guidelines: Leaping bass after a tie: read 5–6, not 2–4 (Durante p. 31).
When the bass leaps down a 4th, a passing augmented 4th accompanied by a 6th can be inserted (Durante p. 27).
Ascending by step the bass “takes 5 then 6”; descending by step “7 then 6” (pp. 25–26) — the 5–6 and 7–6 moti.

patterns.name: Diminution: what changes and what stays
patterns.summary: Diminution transforms a slow, chordal (continuo-like) realization into a fast, idiomatic one. The harmony and the voice leading of the simple realization stay; the surface changes. Neapolitan students learnt it by writing endless diminutions over the same cadences, scales and bass motions they used for partimenti, first in slow, species-like values and then in fast scales, arpeggios and passagework.
rules: The diminished line must still realize the same chords and resolve the same dissonances as the plain realization — diminution decorates, it does not reharmonize.
Once a “modo” (style) is chosen for a passage, apply it to every parallel passage (the same bass motion, the same transposed module).
guidelines: A decorated realization differs from a simple one in four ways (Sanguinetti): the right hand moves faster than the harmony; the right-hand line is a polyphonic melody (it alternates between voices of the underlying chords); the left hand may take part in the inner voices; rhythms are complementary between the hands.

Keep two levels apart: the surface rhythm (sixteenths, triplets) and the essential pulse (how often harmony and voice leading change). Abrupt changes of surface rhythm in the bass need a complementary figure in the right hand.

Levels of realization (Fenaroli Books I, II, IV, editor’s notes): block chords → a melody made of chord tones → passing and neighbour notes, motives taken from the bass → prepared dissonances and small figures → extended imitation and counterpoint.
Unfigured basses (Fenaroli Book IV): ask “which pattern is this?” rather than “which chord comes next?”.
Rhythmic continuity is the norm in Durante’s generation: once the right hand starts in eighths or sixteenths it keeps going, except at grace notes and cadences.

patterns.name: Catalogue of diminution techniques in Durante’s Diminuiti
patterns.summary: Durante’s diminuiti are wordless; the techniques below are what the styles (modi) actually do. The numbers point to the collection so you can study each one.
guidelines: Arpeggiation of the continuo chords (No. 1 Style 1; Sanguinetti Ex. 12.2).
Scalar runs that fill the space between chord tones (No. 1 Style 2).
Fast alternation of two voices, a violinistic figure (No. 7, Romanesca; Style 2 adds a 7–6).
Turns and neighbour figures over each bass note (No. 9 Style 1; triplets in Style 2).

Patterns that carry an interval progression: 5–6 (No. 9 Style 3, Nos. 12, 28; on the last eighth of each bass note in No. 51), parallel 6ths (No. 62 Style 2), parallel 3rds/10ths with the bass (Nos. 9, 58).

A leading tone placed before each new chord root (Nos. 43, 54); chromatic circles of fifths (No. 22 Style 5, Nos. 89–90). Leading tones accompanied by a diminished 5th that contracts to a 3rd (No. 73).
Fa–mi in the right hand against mi–fa in the bass, across the barline (Nos. 25, 26).
Call and response between soprano and alto, or between melody and bass (Nos. 36, 70, 83, 102).
Anticipating or echoing the bass motive in the right hand (Nos. 60, 76, 90, 92, 94) — the step from diminution to imitation.
Time stretching: the same chords spread over more or fewer bars (Nos. 64, 67, 68) — preparation for the free treatment of time in fugues.
Disguised basses: octave displacement of every other note, reordered steps, a note held from weak to strong beat implying a 4/2 (Nos. 50, 62, 87, 91, 100).

patterns.name: Diminutions of the leading tone → tonic bass (mi–fa)
patterns.summary: Durante opens the collection with the commonest bass of all, the rising semitone ⑦→①, and shows three manners of decorating it: an arpeggio rising through the dominant chord and falling by step to the tonic’s 3rd; a scale descending a 10th; and chords in the right hand while the left hand breaks the bass into octaves.
rules: Whatever the figuration, the outer frame stays: ⑦ carries a 6 (or 6/5), the line lands on the 3rd of ①.
guidelines: The ⑦→① bass often leads into a compound cadence (No. 2) or a simple cadence in triple time (No. 4).
In minor the same figures apply with the raised ⑦ (No. 6).

patterns.name: Diminutions over the moti del basso
patterns.summary: Most of the Diminuiti decorate the standard bass motions (movimenti) — the same ones Fenaroli lists in his Rules and Furno sets in three parts. Learn one or two manners for each motion and you can apply them in any partimento.
rules: Identify the movimento first (reduce octave displacements and reorderings), then choose a manner.
guidelines: Rising scale: 3–2–1 turns or 5–6 on each note (Nos. 9, 12, 13, 14, 28, 51, 64, 92); fast versions sound like fauxbourdon 6/3s (No. 13).
Up a 3rd, down a step: alternating 5/3 and 6/3, or 8–7 / 6 with passing 7ths (Nos. 11, 15, 16, 17, 20, 29, 44); with 7–6 suspensions (No. 98).
Down a 3rd, up a step: 6/3 or 6/5/3 on the second note (Nos. 50, 59, 72, 77–78 — fourteen treatments in all —, 91, 100, 102, 103).
Up a 4th, down a 3rd: Nos. 19, 21, 23, 30, 40, 52, 53. Up a 4th, down a 5th (circle of fifths): Nos. 16, 22 (diatonic and chromatic), 89.
Up a 5th, down a 4th: Nos. 24, 31 (passing 4/2), 43, 54, 62, 81, 88, 96. Up a 6th, down a 5th: Nos. 32–35, 80, 83, 93.
Descending 6/3 chords with 7–6 or implied 7ths: Nos. 71, 101, 103. Descending tetrachords: Nos. 42, 94, 95. Romanesca: Nos. 7, 8, 79, 99. Rising chromatic bass: Nos. 27, 55; falling: No. 75.
